Creative Writing | Unit 1 | Lesson 1 | Page 1 of 6

Lesson Overview: Creative Writing Identity and Workshop Norms

Lesson Focus

Lesson 1: Creative Writing Identity and Workshop Norms

Primary Standard: MLA.CW.COM.02 — Peer Feedback and Collaborative Techniques.

Supporting Standards: MLA.CW.COM.04 — Academic Language for ELLs; MLA.CW.COM.05 — Social and Instructional Communication for ELLs.

What You Will Learn

  • Explain how creative writers collect, develop, test, and revise ideas.
  • Use a writer’s notebook as evidence of observation, experimentation, and reflection.
  • Distinguish useful craft feedback from praise, judgment, commands, and vague advice.
  • Use specific evidence and respectful academic language during a workshop.

Why This Matters

Creative writing helps you communicate ideas, experiences, and perspectives with purpose. Each lesson strengthens your ability to read like a writer, make deliberate craft choices, revise thoughtfully, and explain how those choices affect a reader. These skills build creative confidence, clear communication, and responsible participation in a writing community.

What You Will Do

  • Learn and apply the lesson vocabulary.
  • Follow step-by-step instruction and study worked examples.
  • Practice through interactive checks and guided application.
  • Complete Independent Work to apply the lesson skills.
  • Complete a separate Checkpoint to demonstrate your understanding.

Lesson Workflow

  1. Complete Pages 1–4 in order.
  2. Complete Page 5 and submit it with your Page 2 vocabulary in Notebook Evidence Submission.
  3. Complete Page 6 and submit it separately in Checkpoint Submission.
  4. Review TOR feedback, correct errors, and resubmit any work scoring below 80%.
  5. Complete the assessment listed after the lesson. A score of at least 80% is required.

page.title: Vocabulary and Definitions
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 1 | Lesson 1 | Page 2 of 6

Vocabulary and Definitions

Notebook Task

Record every core term and its complete meaning in your notebook. Submit these vocabulary notes with your Independent Work as Notebook Evidence. Use the examples to see how each term works in context. Reference glossary terms do not need to be copied.

TermMeaningExample
creative writingOriginal writing shaped through deliberate choices in language, image, structure, voice, character, and form to create an intended effect.A writer reshapes a true memory into a scene that emphasizes uncertainty.
writer’s notebookA working record of observations, questions, experiments, drafts, feedback, and revision plans—not merely a collection of finished work.You collect a line of dialogue, a sensory detail, and two possible openings.
workshopA structured exchange in which writers share drafts, listen actively, discuss craft evidence, and use feedback to make their own revision decisions.A group names what a draft does, asks questions, and offers revision possibilities.
craft choiceA deliberate decision about diction, imagery, detail, structure, voice, tone, pacing, character, dialogue, or form.The writer replaces “walked” with “stumbled” to suggest exhaustion.
feedbackA specific response that identifies draft evidence, explains its effect, and offers a focused possibility for revision.“The abrupt final sentence creates surprise; consider echoing its image earlier.”
active listeningAttentive listening that seeks to understand the writer’s purpose before responding, interrupting, or proposing changes.A reader first asks, “What effect did you want here?”
reader effectThe thought, feeling, question, expectation, or interpretation produced by a particular craft choice.A repeated ticking sound makes the reader expect time to run out.
revisionPurposeful re-seeing and reshaping of a draft to strengthen meaning, effect, structure, voice, or clarity; it is more than correcting errors.The writer moves the reveal, cuts an explanation, and strengthens a recurring image.

Vocabulary in Action: A Writer at Work

Now apply the eight core terms to a writer-and-reader scenario. Match the action or result named in each example, not simply a word that sounds familiar. Use the definitions above when needed.

Practice only: Check your matches, read the feedback, and retry any mistakes. The displayed score is not a course grade. No screenshot or extra written response is required. Match all eight examples, then use Check to review your answers.

Connect to your writing: On the next page, notice how a craft choice leads to a reader effect, how feedback offers an option, and how revision tests that option. You will use this process in your Independent Work.

Craft Glossary — Use It While You Read

You are not expected to arrive knowing all these terms. First notice the words or action; then use this glossary to find an accurate name. A plain-language observation with evidence is more useful than an impressive label used incorrectly.

Craft terms used in this lesson
TermMeaning and example
writing identityYour developing interests, experiences, questions, and choices as a writer; not a fixed label or a measure of talent.
evidence and inferenceEvidence is what the text actually says or shows. An inference is a reasoned interpretation based on that evidence; it is not automatically a proven fact.
dictionWord choice. “Gripped” suggests a different action or feeling from “held.”
imagery and sensory detailLanguage that evokes sight, sound, touch, taste, or smell. “The rough paper scratched her thumb” uses touch.
personificationGiving a human action or quality to something nonhuman: “the hallway swallowed everyone.”
metaphor and simileA metaphor describes one thing as another without “like” or “as”: light “stitched gold.” A simile makes a comparison using “like” or “as”: sugar “like a small hill.”
contrastA meaningful difference placed side by side, such as a rushing crowd beside a still character.
pacingHow quickly or slowly the reader experiences events. Describing small actions can stretch a brief moment.
dialogue and characterizationDialogue is a character’s spoken words. Characterization is how writing reveals a character through words, actions, thoughts, and details.
subtextMeaning implied beneath the spoken words. A character may say “Fine” while actions suggest discomfort.
ambiguityMore than one plausible meaning or interpretation. Productive ambiguity gives enough evidence to consider alternatives; it is different from missing basic information.
symbolismUsing a concrete object, image, or action to suggest a larger idea. Its meaning must be supported by the passage, not assumed from a universal symbol list.
mood, tone, and voiceMood is the atmosphere or feeling a passage creates for a reader. Tone is the attitude conveyed toward the subject. Voice is the distinctive way a narrator, speaker, or writer sounds.
tension and conflictTension is a sense of uncertainty or pressure. Conflict is a struggle between competing wants, people, or forces; it can happen within a character.
speaker and narrativeThe speaker is the voice speaking in a poem, not necessarily its author. A narrative tells a sequence of connected events.

Make the Vocabulary Work

Choose A or B before opening the feedback.

Which response uses evidence and inference accurately?

A. “She gripped the ticket” is evidence. It may suggest fear, but nearby details are needed to support that inference.
B. “She is afraid of leaving” is evidence because gripping always proves fear.
Check your choice and reasoning

A is stronger. It separates the exact words in the sentence from a possible interpretation. B confuses an inference with evidence and treats one action as proof of only one emotion; gripping could also suggest anger, excitement, or urgency.

page.title: Lesson
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 1 | Lesson 1 | Page 3 of 6

Direct Teaching: From Writer’s Notebook to Useful Feedback

Begin with Noticing, Not Judging

Let’s begin as writers before we respond as readers. Imagine noticing a person turn an old key over in a pocket. I do not yet have a plot. I have an action worth exploring. Instead of deciding that my idea is too ordinary, I record what I can observe and ask a question about it.

Here is a model notebook entry. Read down the left column to follow my process. Read across to see both the writing and the reason behind my choice.

Model notebook entry: an ordinary key
MoveNotebook entryWhy I do this
ObserveA thumb rubs the smooth edge of an old key.I record a visible action before inventing its cause.
WonderWhat if the key opens a place the character is not ready to revisit?A question gives the observation a possible direction. It is invention, not a fact about a real person.
ExperimentAt the gate, I rubbed the key smooth side up. I could still turn back.I test first-person voice and a delayed action rather than explain the entire past.
ReflectThe hesitation interests me more than the gate. I want to explore why familiar places can feel unfamiliar.I identify an interest that may shape my writing identity.
Set a goalLet the reader sense hesitation without explaining its cause yet.This purpose will help me choose useful feedback and revision.

Your notebook can include unfinished trials and crossed-out ideas. That is evidence of thinking, not failure. Choose a safe or invented object and jot an observation, a “What if?” question, and a possible writing goal. Keep these as practice notes you may use on Page 5.

Workshop Norms: Protect the Writer and Study the Draft

A workshop is not a vote on whether a writer is talented. It is a conversation about what a draft currently does. We can question a sentence without judging the person who wrote it. The writer owns the final decision.

  1. Ask permission and purpose: “What would you like me to notice?” The writer may choose an invented piece and does not owe readers private background information.
  2. Listen without interrupting: Paraphrase the goal: “You want tension, but you want the reason to remain uncertain.” Ask whether you understood correctly.
  3. Discuss the text, not the person: Say what words or actions led to your response. Do not assume a narrator’s life is the author’s life.
  4. Offer, do not take over: Suggest a test. The writer can accept it, adapt it, or decline it with a reason.

Teacher reminder: If you work alone, use the supplied draft and practice both roles. You do not need a classmate to complete this lesson.

Knowledge Check: Protect the Writer

Situation: A writer says, “I want the reader to feel uncertain about whether Mara will open the door.” Which response follows the workshop norms and gives the writer something useful to test?

A. “Mara should open the door immediately because waiting makes the scene boring.”

B. “The pause before Mara reaches the handle creates uncertainty. If you want that uncertainty to last longer, you might add one sound from behind the door before she decides.”

Choose A or B before opening the explanation. Look for four parts: evidence, craft choice, reader effect, and an optional revision connected to the writer’s goal.

Check your choice and reasoning

B is stronger. It points to the pause, explains how the pause affects the reader, and offers a small experiment that supports the writer’s stated purpose. A is weaker because it replaces the writer’s goal with the reader’s preferred plot and calls the scene boring without citing evidence.

The Four-Step Feedback Process

Read the draft once for the situation before hunting for techniques. Then read again with a pencil or a note beside you. The sequence below keeps your response anchored to the writing.

Feedback route: follow the numbered steps
StepQuestion to askUseful sentence opening
1. Locate evidenceWhich exact words or action caused my response?“In the words…”
2. Name the craft choiceWhat is the writer doing with those words?“The repeated action / image / dialogue…”
3. Explain the reader effectWhat does it make me infer, feel, notice, or expect—and why?“This makes me… because…”
4. Offer a focused optionWhat could the writer test to support the stated goal?“If you want…, you might try…”

The steps are not four disconnected labels. Build a chain: words in the draft → a craft choice → a reasoned reader response → a purposeful revision option. A writer cannot act on “make it better.” A writer can test “delay the reply with one physical action.”

Watch Me Read a Single Sentence

Sentence: “Her key stopped an inch from the lock.”

First, I locate evidence. I underline “stopped an inch.” I can point to those words; I am not yet making a claim about the character’s past.

Next, I name the choice. The writer pauses an action just before it is complete. This controls pacing—how fast the reader experiences the event. A tiny distance gets its own moment, so we wait with the character.

Now, I explain the effect. I wonder why she hesitates because she is close enough to unlock the door but does not finish. Notice the word “because”: it connects my response to evidence. I cannot responsibly announce that someone dangerous is inside; the sentence does not establish that.

Finally, I consider purpose. Suppose the writer wants hesitation without revealing its cause. I might say: “The pause in ‘stopped an inch’ slows the moment and makes me expect a difficult choice. You might add one touch detail, such as the key pressing into her palm, to make the hesitation physical while keeping its cause uncertain.”

I have offered a possible test, not a required rewrite. Another reader may suggest a sound. The writer should compare each option with the intended effect.

Pause and Choose: Evidence or Assumption

Compare the two explanations before selecting an answer. Feedback appears immediately after your choice. Read why one interpretation is better supported and why the other goes too far. You can retry; this practice does not count toward your course grade.

Take the strategy with you: Notice the detail → explain what it may suggest → acknowledge what remains unknown. No additional written submission is required.

Three Craft Choices You Will Meet

Personification: “The hallway swallowed everyone.” A hallway cannot literally swallow. The writer gives it an action associated with a living being, making the crowd’s movement seem forceful. Name the action first; then explain its effect.

Metaphor and contrast: “Morning stitched gold along the cracked sill.” A sill is the ledge at the bottom of a window. Light becomes a kind of stitching. “Cracked” introduces damage, while “stitched” suggests repair. The meaning comes from the relationship between the words, not from calling the line “pretty.”

Subtext: “‘Fine,’ Mateo said, folding the permission slip into smaller squares.” The spoken word suggests agreement, but the repeated action may suggest discomfort. Subtext is this implied meaning beneath the speech. We still need context before deciding whether he is angry, worried, or reluctant.

Symbolism without guessing: An object can suggest more than its practical use when the surrounding actions or memories support that meaning. A key might suggest access in one story and an unwanted responsibility in another. Never assume that an object has one fixed meaning in every text.

Knowledge Check: Explain the Craft Choice

Sentence: “Fine,” Mateo said, folding the permission slip into smaller squares.

Which analysis shows the stronger evidence-to-reasoning chain?

A. “The contrast between Mateo’s word and his repeated folding may suggest discomfort because his action does not match the calm agreement of ‘Fine.’ The exact emotion remains uncertain.”

B. “Mateo is angry with his parents and plans to refuse permission because folding paper always symbolizes rebellion.”

Choose A or B. Test each answer by asking: What does the sentence actually show? What can reasonably be inferred? What remains unknown?

Check your choice and reasoning

A is stronger. It uses both the spoken word and the physical action, explains the contrast, and keeps the inference appropriately qualified. B is weaker because it invents parents, a plan, and a fixed symbolic meaning that the sentence does not establish.

Helpful Uncertainty or Simple Confusion?

Sometimes a writer deliberately leaves more than one interpretation possible. That is ambiguity. Before asking the writer to explain everything, ask: Do I understand what is happening but wonder what it means? Or am I unable to follow who is speaking or acting?

Decide what kind of clarification is needed
Reader experienceUseful response
I understand the action but can support two emotions.Ask about the intended effect. Preserve uncertainty if it serves the writer’s goal.
I cannot tell which character said the line.Suggest clarifying the speaker before adding an explanation of feelings.

Rigor means considering alternatives and defending a choice with evidence. It does not mean inventing a complicated interpretation that the passage cannot support.

Compare Feedback Before You Give It

From judgment to usable feedback
Weak responseMore useful responseWhy it helps
“I liked it.”“The pause before the key turns makes me anticipate a difficult choice.”Names a specific strength and its effect.
“Make her confess.”“I cannot tell what she wants in this exchange. Could one action make her immediate goal clearer?”Identifies a reader difficulty without choosing the plot for the author.
“Add more description.”“If you want the pause to feel longer, you might add one touch detail before she turns the key.”Offers a small, testable change tied to purpose.

A response to a strength does not always need a correction. Explain what is working so the author knows what to preserve. When a task asks for revision advice, add a focused option instead of inventing a flaw.

Try the Method Before the Full Examples

Pause and try: For Jon’s invitation sentence above, improve “This is confusing.” Name the uncertainty, connect it to the text, and offer an optional move.

Check your thinking — open after you try

One possible response: “Jon’s smile seems to conflict with hiding the invitation, so I wonder whether he is pretending to welcome it. If you want that conflict to be clearer, you might add a small change in his expression after the invitation disappears.” This preserves the author’s choice of motive. It is not the only valid answer.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other choice before continuing. Compare both explanations so you can name why the stronger answer works.

If you got stuck: Return to the exact words. Name what you can see before interpreting it. Use the craft glossary if a label is unfamiliar, and try the sentence opening “This makes me wonder… because…”.

Before moving on: Can you explain the difference between evidence and inference? Can you offer a suggestion without deciding the plot? Page 4 will show how the same process changes across three kinds of writing.

Contact your Teacher of Record (TOR) if you need clarification, feedback, or support. Ask for help as soon as you need it.

page.title: Worked Example
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 1 | Lesson 1 | Page 4 of 6

Worked Example: Making the Thinking Visible

Read Like an Apprentice Writer

We will examine three short drafts. For each, first read the passage without the explanation. Ask yourself, “Which words made me react?” Then compare your thinking with mine. You do not have to produce my exact interpretation; you do need a clear link between the words and your response.

In Example 1, we will also follow the writer’s decision through a complete revision cycle. In Examples 2 and 3, notice how the writer’s purpose changes which advice is useful.

Example 1 — Narrative Image and Pacing

Draft: “The last bell rang. The hallway swallowed everyone at once. Mira stayed beside the dented locker, counting to ten before she touched the envelope.”

Task: Give feedback that helps the writer strengthen tension.

Teacher think-aloud: Notice that the hallway cannot literally swallow people. “Swallowed” turns the space into an active force. Now compare “everyone at once” with Mira counting to ten. The crowd moves quickly; Mira delays. I notice her hesitation because the two speeds are placed beside each other. I will not invent the contents of the envelope to explain it.

  1. Locate evidence: “the hallway swallowed everyone” and Mira’s delayed touch.
  2. Name choices: personification, contrast, and slowed action.
  3. Reason through the effect: The rushing hallway makes Mira’s stillness noticeable; counting delays the envelope reveal and creates tension.
  4. Choose a revision priority: The tension is already working. If the writer wants to make the hesitation more physical, one sensory cue could be a useful experiment—not an automatic requirement.

Model feedback: “The personification in ‘the hallway swallowed everyone’ makes the crowd feel forceful, while Mira’s counting slows the moment and builds tension. You might add one sound or touch detail from the envelope so the reader feels the hesitation physically while its cause stays uncertain.”

Why it works: The response uses two pieces of evidence, explains their relationship, and proposes a focused option without deciding what the envelope contains.

Example 1 Continued — Feedback Becomes a Revision

Annotation map: words → craft → reader effect
Exact evidenceCraft choiceReasoned effect
“the hallway swallowed everyone”PersonificationThe movement seems forceful because the hallway is described as if it could consume the crowd.
“everyone at once” / “counting to ten”Contrast and pacingThe crowd’s speed highlights Mira’s delay, so attention shifts to her hesitation.

1. The writer sets the goal: “I want the reader to feel Mira’s hesitation without learning what the envelope contains.”

2. The reader offers feedback: The model above suggests one sound or touch detail. It explains why that might support the goal.

3. The writer decides: “I will test a touch detail. I will not add the envelope’s contents, because that would remove the uncertainty I want.” Notice that the writer selects and adapts an option.

Before and after: only the final sentence changes
Original sentenceRevised sentence
Mira stayed beside the dented locker, counting to ten before she touched the envelope.Mira stayed beside the dented locker, counting to ten before she touched the envelope; its rough edge scraped her thumb, and she loosened her grip.

4. Read the complete revised draft: “The last bell rang. The hallway swallowed everyone at once. Mira stayed beside the dented locker, counting to ten before she touched the envelope; its rough edge scraped her thumb, and she loosened her grip.”

5. Compare the effect: Read both versions aloud, or track the actions silently. The revision adds two small actions—scraping and loosening—before the scene moves on. These extend the pause and make the contact physical. We still do not know the envelope’s contents. That matches the stated goal.

6. Judge the trade-off: More detail is not always better. The revision is longer and may feel slower than necessary. If the writer wants a sharper, faster ending, the original could be preferable. A strong revision explanation names the intended effect and the evidence of change; it does not simply say “I added description.”

Pause and Choose: Explain the Revision

Which response best explains why the revision may be stronger?

A. “My revision is better because it is longer.”
Weaker response. Length is only a measurable change; it does not explain what the new detail does for the reader or whether it supports the writer’s goal.
B. “The touch detail extends Mira’s hesitation without revealing the envelope’s contents.”
Stronger response. It identifies the exact change, connects it to pacing and reader experience, and tests the revision against the stated goal of preserving uncertainty.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other response. Compare both explanations and name what makes the stronger reasoning useful.

Example 2 — Poetic Image and Ambiguity

Draft:

Morning stitched gold
along the cracked sill—
a bright repair
that vanished when I moved.

Word help: A sill is the ledge at the bottom of a window. Ambiguity means more than one plausible interpretation; here, the apparent repair may feel hopeful, temporary, or both.

Task: Respond to the image without flattening its ambiguity.

Teacher think-aloud: I first picture sunlight on a damaged window ledge. Then I notice that “stitched” belongs to sewing and repair, not literal sunlight. That metaphor lets light seem helpful. But “vanished” prevents me from treating the repair as permanent. I should hold both pieces of evidence together instead of announcing that the poem is simply happy.

  1. Locate evidence: “stitched gold,” “cracked,” “repair,” and “vanished.”
  2. Name choices: metaphor, contrast, and an image that changes.
  3. Consider more than one meaning: The light may suggest hope, but its disappearance may also suggest that the repair is temporary or imagined.
  4. Protect productive ambiguity: Feedback should help sustain the tension rather than force one explanation.

Model feedback: “The metaphor ‘stitched gold’ makes the light seem capable of repairing damage, but ‘vanished’ makes that repair uncertain. The contrast leaves me deciding whether the speaker feels hopeful or unconvinced. You might echo either ‘stitch’ or ‘crack’ in the next image so the tension continues without explaining it away.”

Why it works: The response acknowledges multiple defensible interpretations and bases each one on diction—specific word choices.

Pause and Choose: Protect the Ambiguity

Which feedback better preserves the poem’s tension between hope and uncertainty?

A. “End by saying the speaker feels hopeful so readers know the correct meaning.”
Weaker response. This forces one interpretation and may erase the tension created by “repair” and “vanished.” It also decides the poem’s meaning for the writer.
B. “If you want the uncertainty to continue, consider echoing ‘stitch’ or ‘crack’ in the next image without explaining which feeling wins.”
Stronger response. It links an optional revision to the writer’s possible goal, uses the established image pattern, and leaves both evidence-based interpretations available.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other response. Compare both explanations and name what makes the stronger reasoning useful.

Example 3 — Dialogue, Action, and Subtext

Draft: “‘Fine,’ Mateo said. He folded the permission slip in half, then in half again, pressing each crease with his thumbnail. ‘Tell her I signed it.’”

Task: Help the writer clarify character emotion without naming it directly.

Teacher think-aloud: Start with the word “Fine.” By itself, it might communicate agreement. Now read the repeated folding and pressure of the thumbnail. Those actions complicate the word. This is subtext: a meaning implied beneath the speech. I can support discomfort, but I cannot prove its cause. Before requesting a clearer emotion, I would ask, “Should readers recognize one feeling here, or remain uncertain?”

  1. Locate evidence: “Fine,” repeated folding, pressure from the thumbnail, and “Tell her.”
  2. Name choices: dialogue-action contrast, repetition, and an indirect request.
  3. Infer carefully: Mateo may be angry, reluctant, or anxious; the draft supports tension but not one certain emotion.
  4. Suggest a discriminating detail: One additional behavior or tonal cue could narrow the reader’s inference.

Model feedback: “Mateo says ‘Fine,’ but the repeated folding and hard creases contradict the word and create subtext. I can tell he is tense, though I cannot yet distinguish anger from worry. You might add one precise vocal or physical detail that points toward the emotion you intend while keeping it unstated.”

Why it works: The feedback distinguishes evidence from inference and asks for precision without rewriting Mateo’s reaction. A vocal cue means a detail about how the words sound, such as a whisper or a broken phrase. If uncertainty is the author’s goal, the existing actions may already be enough.

Pause and Choose: Keep the Claim Within the Evidence

Which interpretation is supported without inventing Mateo’s relationship or exact emotion?

A. “Mateo is definitely angry with his mother because folding paper always symbolizes rebellion.”
Weaker response. The passage does not identify “her” as Mateo’s mother, prove anger, or establish a universal meaning for folded paper. The claim goes beyond the evidence.
B. “Mateo’s repeated folding and hard creases suggest tension despite his calm word ‘Fine,’ though the cause remains uncertain.”
Stronger response. It uses the contrast between dialogue and action, qualifies the inference with “suggest,” and clearly states what the reader still cannot know.

Retry: If your first choice is weaker, close it and select the other response. Compare both explanations and name what makes the stronger reasoning useful.

Comparison: Weak vs. Useful

Weak: “Make all three pieces more descriptive.”

Useful: Each model above identifies a different craft problem—sensory tension, sustained ambiguity, or emotional subtext. Effective feedback responds to the specific purpose and evidence of a draft rather than applying the same generic advice to every genre.

Your Turn Before Independent Work

New practice line: “Ari placed two cups on the table, then returned one to the cupboard when the doorbell rang.”

Pause and try: Write two or three sentences: quote an action, name a craft choice, explain a possible effect, and offer one optional revision tied to a goal. Do not invent the visitor’s identity.

Check your thinking — open after you try

One possible response: “Returning one cup just as the doorbell rings interrupts the preparation and creates uncertainty about Ari’s expectations. If you want the change of mind to feel more tense, you might pause Ari’s hand above the cup before it is removed.” The action supplies evidence; interrupted action names a choice; uncertainty explains an effect; and the last sentence offers a purposeful option.

Ready to apply: On Page 5, use this process with a new passage and your own scene. Your ideas should be your own; use the models for the reasoning process, not sentences to copy.

🧑‍🏫 TOR Help

Contact your Teacher of Record (TOR) if you need clarification, feedback, or support. Ask for help as soon as you need it.

page.title: Independent Work
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 1 | Lesson 1 | Page 5 of 6

Independent Work: Notice, Choose, Write, Revise

Purpose and Directions

Apply the lesson skills by reading like a workshop partner, making one evidence-based craft judgment, writing a focused scene, and revising one purposeful choice. Complete each numbered task and submit it with your vocabulary notes in Notebook Evidence Submission.

Quality matters more than length: make each response specific, supported, and useful.

Draft for Workshop: “The Blue Bowl”

Leah found the bowl behind the flour tin, where her grandmother used to hide birthday money. Its blue glaze had faded at the rim, and one hairline crack ran from the base to a painted swallow. She set it on the counter before her brother arrived.

“You kept that?” Daniel asked.

Leah turned the bowl until the crack faced the wall. “It was already here.”

Rain tapped the kitchen window. Daniel opened a drawer, closed it, then opened the next one. He had come for the recipe cards, but neither of them said so. Leah remembered their grandmother measuring sugar without a cup, letting the white grains rise in her palm like a small hill.

Daniel reached toward the bowl and stopped. “Mom said we should divide everything.”

“Then take the cards.” Leah heard how quickly she answered. She placed both hands around the bowl, though it was empty.

1. Notice and Plan

Complete this organizer with brief notes. Use exact evidence before making an inference.

Exact word, action, or detailWhat it suggestsCraft choice
   

Then explain in two or three sentences what is happening between Leah and Daniel. Clearly distinguish what the passage states from what you infer.

2. Choose the Stronger Workshop Response

Read both responses. Record A or B, then explain in two or three sentences why your choice would be more useful to the writer. Consider evidence, craft language, reader effect, and respect. The answer is not revealed on this page.

A. “I like the bowl because it is interesting. The writer should add more details and make the characters explain what happened.”
B. “When Leah turns the crack toward the wall, the action indirectly shows that she wants to protect or hide something connected to the bowl. That makes the tension feel restrained because the characters avoid naming the conflict. If the writer wants the tension slightly stronger, they might add one precise physical reaction from Daniel before he speaks.”

3. Apply the Craft in Your Writing

Choose a safe or invented object that matters to a character. Write one goal sentence stating what you want the reader to feel or wonder. Then write a focused six-to-eight-sentence scene.

Use at least two purposeful craft choices—such as action, dialogue, sensory detail, pacing, or placement of the object—to suggest emotion without directly naming it. Your scene should have a clear situation and remain your own original work.

4. Revise and Explain

Original sentenceRevised sentenceWhat changed and why
   

Revise one sentence from your scene so it better supports your goal. Explain how the change should affect the reader. Do not rewrite the entire scene.

Before You Submit

  • I completed every numbered task.
  • I used exact evidence before making an inference.
  • I explained my A/B choice.
  • I wrote an original scene with purposeful craft choices.
  • I revised one sentence and explained my reasoning.

🧑‍🏫 TOR Help

Contact your Teacher of Record (TOR) if you need clarification, feedback, or support. Ask for help as soon as you need it.

page.title: Checkpoint
page.contents:
Creative Writing | Unit 1 | Lesson 1 | Page 6 of 6

Checkpoint: Creative Writing Identity and Workshop Norms

Your Purpose

Demonstrate that you can develop an observation into organized creative writing and respond to a draft with specific, respectful, goal-based feedback.

Complete all four parts independently. A score of at least 80% is required.

New Source: “The Last Chair”

Writer’s goal: Make the reader sense that Eli is delaying an important decision without explaining the decision yet.

The custodian had stacked every chair except one. Eli sat in it, turning a bus token between his fingers. The metal had warmed against his palm, but the number stamped across its face still looked unfamiliar.

“Building closes in five,” the custodian called.

Eli nodded as if five minutes were an answer. Beyond the glass doors, the Route 6 bus sighed at the curb. He slid the token into his pocket, removed it, and placed it on the empty desk beside him. When the bus pulled away, he did not watch it go. He watched the token stop spinning.

Bus token: a small coin-like object once used to pay for a bus ride.

1. Analyze the Writing

  1. Evidence and effect: Identify two exact details that create hesitation. For each detail, name the craft choice and explain what it makes the reader infer, feel, notice, or expect.
  2. Evidence and uncertainty: Explain what the passage supports about Eli’s situation and what remains unknown. Do not turn an inference into a fact.
Exact wordsCraft choiceReader effect and reasoning

3. Create an Organized Scene

Writing situation: A character waits outside a closed shop while holding an unopened envelope. The character must decide whether to leave it, open it, or take it away.

Write a 250–350 word original scene. Follow this structure:

  1. Opening paragraph—hook and context: Begin with a concrete action, image, sound, or line of dialogue. Establish the place, the envelope, and the character’s immediate situation. Do not explain the entire history.
  2. Development paragraph—build tension: Use at least two sensory details and one repeated action or image. Let those details reveal hesitation and guide the reader’s attention.
  3. Turning-point paragraph—force a choice: Introduce a new event, discovery, person, or time pressure. Show the character thinking through action, dialogue, or subtext rather than a long explanation.
  4. Closing paragraph—resolve and suggest meaning: Show the character’s decision and immediate consequence. End with an image or action that helps the reader infer why the choice matters.

Keep writer ownership: The structure guides your organization, but the character, circumstances, voice, and meaning must be your own.
